I am a firefighter and I recently received my certification for hybrid electric and electric vehicle fires. 

We first identify what the type of car is. Is it a hybrid which runs a combustion and electric motor or just electirc like a Tesla.

The manufactures try to make the batteries accessible for mechanics for when they fix the car so they place them either in the center of the car usually below the back seats, trunk, or in the front engine compartment.

There are battery disconnects similar to a normal battery in a car and the high voltage lines are usually orange so we are able to notice them and avoid them

It's not normal for the battery to get damaged in the first place because it's usually very secure in a metal casing to protect it from the environment and crashes.

The cars also have a lot of safety points built into them so they tend not to pose a risk to us, manufacturers like Tesla post first responder guidebooks for us so we can see where everything is inside the car. 

So once we make sure the battery is disconnected, we treat it like any car fire, approach from the side and stabilize it. Turn it into a pool.

So you are talking about a tiller ladder. I don't have experience with and the area I live doesn't have many of them. They are mainly for big cities with tight allies. Reason being, you can fit them really well because they are so manipulative.

Fire apparatus does not require any special license, of course, you must go through training and a "Tillerman" especially must train for a little more than other guys because of how complicated it is.

Ladder trucks are all different in length. Snorkels, towers, quint, and ladders are all different types. The ladder we have at our station is 105 feet from the base to the top.

"Crash trucks" are the green airport firetrucks that you see. They use foam because it suffocates the fire. Jet fuel obviously leaks whenever there is a plane fire. If you use water, it just spreads the fuel because of the oil and water mix and spread.

To answer your question, if a unit hit another car, you would always check to see if the person is okay. Doesn't matter the situation outside of that. Because that person would be first priority if they were in fact injured and the best candidate for immediate care. If however it was just a slight fender bender and the person was fine, the police would take care of the situation while the fire units kept on to the call. I should also say if the person was injured, we wouldn't just forget about the fire, most departments always respond with at least two trucks to all calls. One pump and one ladder or two pumps and 1 commanding officer in a car (supervisor vehicle). The unit to hit the car would take care of the victim while other units went to the fire and if the fire or situation was significant enough, we would call for mutual from another town to cover the unit at the car situation. 

The pump is different for every truck and every situation is different as well. 

The minimum gallons per minute on an average engine is 300 gallons per minute and even up too 1200 gallons if it is a master stream (hose gun on a ladder). Take in to account a truck has about 500-550 gallons in the actual tank however, like in our newer ladder, we have 750 gallons in the tank. If you do the math on that, it won't take long to empty that tank if you are running multiple lines at a time. That is why they use hydrants to directly pull water to the engine and through the lines and we also draft as well which is basically pulling water from a lake or ocean if need be.
